[{:db/id 17592186124445 :knowledge-point/questions ["question-320a3cd2-acfa-559d-b91b-9bfb6f0a3cde"] :db/ensure [:knowledge-point/validate]} {:db/id "question-320a3cd2-acfa-559d-b91b-9bfb6f0a3cde" :question/id #uuid "320a3cd2-acfa-559d-b91b-9bfb6f0a3cde" :question/math-academy-id "q-71231" :question/problem "The curve $C$ is the intersection of a surface $S,$ defined by $z=f(x,y),$ with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Given that the point $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ lies on $C$, and that ${f}_{x}=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)\operatorname{cos}⁡y$, which of the following gives a tangent vector to $C$ at $P?$" :question/worked-solution "The curve $C$ is the intersection of the surface with the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4}.$ Hence, the slope of the tangent to the curve $C$ at the point $P$ will be given by the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}).$ 

To get the slope, we evaluate the partial derivative ${f}_{x}(x,y)$ at $(1,\frac{\pi }{4}):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & =\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\cdot \frac{\pi }{4})\operatorname{cos}⁡\frac{\pi }{4} \\  & =\sqrt{2}\cdot 1\cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(1,\frac{\pi }{4}) & ={f}_{x}(1,\frac{\pi }{4})(x-1) \\ z-0 & =1(x-1) \\ z & =x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(1,\frac{\pi }{4},0)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}y=\frac{\pi }{4} \\ z=x-1\end{aligned}
$$

Next, notice that:

- For the plane $y=\frac{\pi }{4},$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨0,1,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=x-1$ (or $x-z+-1=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨1,0,-1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨0,1,0⟩\times ⟨1,0,-1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ 1 & 0 & -1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-i-k \\  & =⟨-1,0,-1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since $⟨-1,0,-1⟩$ is parallel to the tangent line, then $-⟨-1,0,-1⟩=⟨1,0,1⟩$ is also parallel to it." :question/difficulty :question.difficulty/hard :question/answer-fields $$
\begin{aligned}{f}_{y}(-2,-6) & =\frac{-6-(-2)}{\sqrt{(-2)(-6+(-2))}} \\  & =\frac{-4}{\sqrt{16}} \\  & =-\frac{4}{4} \\  & =-1\end{aligned}
$$

 

Now, we use the point-slope form of a straight line:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-f(-2,-6) & ={f}_{y}(-2,-6)(y-(-6)) \\ z-1 & =-1(y+6) \\ z-1 & =-y-6 \\ z & =-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent line to the curve $C$ at $P(-2,-6,1)$ can be given as the intersection of two planes:

$$
{\begin{aligned}x=-2 \\ z=-y-5\end{aligned}
$$

- For the plane $x=-2,$ a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{1}=⟨1,0,0⟩.$

- For the plane $z=-y-5$ (or $y+z+5=0$), a normal vector to the plane is ${n}_{2}=⟨0,1,1⟩.$

Finally, to find a direction vector for the tangent line, we calculate the cross product of these normal vectors:

$$
\begin{aligned}{n}_{1}\times {n}_{2} & =⟨1,0,0⟩\times ⟨0,1,1⟩ \\  & =\left|\begin{aligned}i & j & k \\ 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 1\end{aligned}\right| \\  & =-j+k \\  & =⟨0,-1,1⟩\end{aligned}
$$

To illustrate, consider the surface $z = f (x, y)= 18 - x^2 - y^2$ and the plane $x=3.$ The intersection of the surface and the plane forms a downward parabolic curve, as shown below. A point $P(3,2,5)$ is plotted and a tangent line is drawn through that point.

![](images/86/8619c41cd0caf04ae9ee9bcae61e31739d8da583793a67c1c87e00186c3ac417.png)

To find the slope of the tangent, we can compute the partial derivative $\dfrac{\partial f}{\partial y}$ and evaluate it at $P(3,2,5)\mathbin{:}$

$$
